theme: Rebuke me not in your anger; show me, O LORD, my end
readingInstruction: Read Psalm 38 and Psalm 39. These are two of David’s most honest prayers, about the suffering that comes with sin and with the brevity of life. Read them slowly.
settingTheScene: Psalm 38 is a penitential psalm, “for the memorial offering,” and describes suffering in body and soul because of sin. Psalm 39 is a meditation on the shortness of life, written by a man who tried to hold his tongue and could not. They are placed together here after David’s long reign and the sins and sorrows of the last chapters. Together they describe the weariness of a man who knows his frailty.
observation: “O LORD, rebuke me not in your anger, nor discipline me in your wrath!” (38:1).
“For my iniquities have gone over my head; like a heavy burden, they are too heavy for me” (38:4).
“I am utterly bowed down and prostrate; all the day I go about mourning” (38:6).
“O Lord, all my longing is before you; my sighing is not hidden from you” (38:9).
“For I hope in you, O LORD; it is you, O Lord my God, who will answer” (38:15).
“Make haste to help me, O Lord, my salvation!” (38:22).
“O LORD, make me know my end and what is the measure of my days; let me know how fleeting I am!” (39:4).
“And now, O Lord, for what do I wait? My hope is in you” (39:7).
interpretation:
Psalm 38 is a portrait of sin’s weight. David feels it as a heavy burden, a pain in his body, and a mourning of his soul. His friends and neighbors stand aloof. He is aware of his guilt. And yet he does not despair. In the middle of the psalm, he says, “For I hope in you, O LORD.” This is the same turn we have seen elsewhere: from the weight of the problem to the strength of the one who can solve it.

A significant line is verse 9: “All my longing is before you; my sighing is not hidden from you.” God knows what we cannot put into words. A sigh is a prayer. There are times when we cannot form sentences, and the psalm assures us that God hears even our groans.

Psalm 39 begins with an attempt at silence. David determined to guard his mouth, so as not to sin with his tongue in the presence of the wicked. But the silence burned inside him, and finally he spoke. What he said was a prayer about the brevity of life.

“Make me know my end… let me know how fleeting I am!” It is a startling request. Most of us avoid thinking about death. David asks for awareness. “Behold, you have made my days a few handbreadths, and my lifetime is as nothing before you.” Every person, even at his best, is a mere breath. This is not morbid. It is the beginning of wisdom. Moses prays the same in Psalm 90:12: “Teach us to number our days that we may get a heart of wisdom.”

The turning point is verse 7: “And now, O Lord, for what do I wait? My hope is in you.” If life is a breath, then everything depends on God. The question is where to place hope. David finds the answer in God alone.

The psalm ends in a plea for relief, with the confession that he is a sojourner with God, a guest on earth. Our time here is short. Our home is with him.
connection: Jesus carried our burden of sin: “He himself bore our sins in his body on the tree” (1 Peter 2:24). James 4:14 says, “You are a mist that appears for a little time and then vanishes.” Psalm 39:12 is echoed in Hebrews 11:13 and 1 Peter 2:11, where believers are “sojourners and exiles.” Paul says, “We look not to the things that are seen but to the things that are unseen” (2 Corinthians 4:18).
application:
Spend a few minutes asking God to “number your days.” What would you do differently if you took your mortality seriously?

Bring a sigh to God today, something you cannot put into words.

Recall that you are a sojourner. Where have you been settling in too deeply?
prayerPrompts: Ask God to teach you to number your days.
Tell him how heavy your iniquities feel and where your hope lies.
